style: Read this as a calm, intimate documentary storyteller. Measured pace, quiet tension, natural pauses between sentences. Not dramatic, not salesy.

paragraphs.cold: In a hospital, there is a moment the staff are trained to catch — the moment a patient quietly begins to die. It hides in a hundred small readings, and it is easy to miss. In twenty eighteen, a machine learned to catch it first. Google took the medical records of a hundred and fourteen thousand people, fed them to an artificial intelligence, and asked it one question: who, in this building, is going to die? It answered with ninety-five per cent accuracy — earlier than the charts, earlier than the nurses, sometimes earlier than the doctor standing at the bed. That result was published in a medical journal. And it leaves a strange question hanging in the air. Why is an advertising company this good at knowing when you will die?
paragraphs.act1: At first, this looks like a story about Google moving into healthcare. But the hospital is almost beside the point. The interesting part is what the machine was already built to do. To see a death coming, it had to be extraordinarily good at one narrow task — take everything known about a person, and work out what happens next. And that skill is the oldest thing Google does. It has spent twenty years perfecting it on the rest of us. This was the same engine, turned to face the final variable.
paragraphs.act2: So how does a company get good enough to forecast a death? By reading all of it. The model read the whole record — the numbers, the scans, and the free-text notes a nurse writes at three in the morning. Forty-six billion data points, for a single set of predictions. And the raw material arrived the way it usually does. A hospital handed Google the records of every patient who came through its doors across seven years, and called them anonymous. The dates were still attached. The doctors' notes were still attached. And to a company that already knows where you were on a given afternoon, a dated, annotated medical file does not stay anonymous for long. The patients were never asked. No one had to ask them.
